This project includes the learning objective from the Artistic Languages core: "To express emotions, ideas, and experiences through art by experimenting with pictorial, graphic, and modeling resources". Throughout the project, they have conducted different experiences and, to conclude, the teacher invites the children to present the creations they have made during this project.  While Martina presents her work, she says: "I made two balls, one yellow and one green, because they are my favorite colors". The teacher asks: "What emotions does your painting express?". Martina responds: "I don't know".  Which of the following teacher's interventions is relevant to help Martina achieve the learning objective?
Answer A: Excellent, Martina! I see your work represents a game with colored balls. Do you like playing with balls? Why is one ball green and the other yellow? Do they remind you of any emotion?
Answer B: Very good job, Martina! The balls you created are in the colors we use to identify emotions. The green represents calm, and the yellow represents joy
Answer C: Great job, Martina! You selected your favorite colors for your work. Can you tell me why you drew balls? What do you feel with the colors green and yellow? Why are they your favorites?
Answer D: Well done, Martina! But would you like to complete your work remembering you need to represent some experience and emotion? It could be the joy of playing ball with your friends or the sadness when you lose the ball
Subdomain: Knowledge of students' understanding and development

Question: In a 5th grade class, a teacher will address the following objective: "To improvise and create musical ideas with a given purpose and an adequate command of musical language." Answer C: The teacher asks the students to listen to a melody and exemplifies various improvisations with different sound elements. Then she asks them to imitate them rhythmically
Answer D: The teacher asks the students to listen to the melody and to play various base rhythms. Then she organizes a rhythmic rondo with the students, alternating their improvisations
Subdomain: Knowledge of teaching and instructional strategies

Question: In a 7th grade, in the instrumental ensemble workshop, the teacher has been working on the interpretation of an arrangement for two voices and instrumental accompaniment. At the end of the presentations, the teacher detects that one group of students makes duration errors in some figures, executing gallops instead of syncopations when these appear in the score.  What formative feedback from the teacher would enable the students to overcome the error and meet the established criteria for the interpretation of the piece?

Question: During a 7th grade class, in the unit on Photography, a teacher is working with her students on the elements of photographic language. Question: A teacher in the first year of high school is working on a vocal piece, specifically a canon in unison for three voices. After explaining this musical procedure, he notices that his students have not fully understood it, so he proposes to use an analogy to facilitate their understanding. What of the following options presents an appropriate analogical comparison to help students understand an execution in unison canon?
Answer A: Imagine that a relay race is being played and the baton is passed to the teammate at the precise moment, and then it is passed to the next one at determined times. The same happens with the melody to sing
Answer B: Imagine that three people are reciting different poems simultaneously at the same speed, fitting and complementing each other, creating a new meaning for the text. In the case of music, the text should be replaced by sung melodies
Answer C: Imagine several audio players with the same melody and then pressing play on each of them with a delay of a certain number of beats. In the case of sung music, each of those players would be a group of singers
Answer D: Imagine that a drawing is made starting with a line in one color from the beginning of the page and then, a certain distance away, another line in a different color is drawn, and so on. The colored lines would be the melodies that should be sung and the centimeters of difference would be the waiting times
Subdomain: Knowledge of teaching and instructional strategies

Question: In a 3rd Grade secondary class, students are working on creations, as the subject teacher has asked them to individually create a small tonal composition. Question: A teacher of a 3rd year secondary class is in the process of staging a choral work with his class. Subdomain: Knowledge of students' understanding and development

Question: A teacher of a 2nd grade secondary class is addressing the reading of a score for an instrumental ensemble that mainly contains groupings of rhythmic figures derived from the quartet of sixteenth notes. Which of the following activities allows addressing the rhythmic reading problem with students and improving the potential transfer of learning to other contexts?

Question: A teacher of a 3rd year high school class sets the goal for students to interpret music with stylistic awareness, technical precision, and fluency. Answer A: Very good interpretation considering the style of the work. However, in vocal music it is important that the text matches the corresponding rhythms, thus they will be able to articulate these aspects together
Answer B: I congratulate you on your fluent interpretation of the piece. Now, it is important that, when interpreting music in voices, the singers listen to each other to achieve greater articulation among them
Answer C: Well done so far; but there is still room for improvement in the interpretation of the work. To verify the correct articulation of the text, I recommend reviewing the reading of the score several times

Question: To start the unit Design and Dissemination, in a 2nd Year secondary class, a teacher conducts a diagnostic assessment to determine the students' approach to design and its different branches. Question: In a 4th year secondary class, during the development of the unit 'Exploring the Artistic Languages of Our Time', the teacher presents works by the experimental photographer Man Ray to the students and explains the concept of a rayogram, defining it as a technique for obtaining images without using a camera.
